questions.s: Concerning the gluteal nerves and vessels (Last's):
o: The superior gluteal nerve has no cutaneous distribution
Unlike the artery, whose superficial branch reaches the skin. (Last's p. 163)
In a positive Trendelenburg test the pelvis falls on the stance side
It falls on the opposite (unsupported) side. (Last's p. 163)
The inferior gluteal nerve enters gluteus maximus towards its medial end
(Last's p. 163)
Piriformis is supplied by the superior gluteal nerve
By anterior rami of S1 and S2. (Last's p. 163)

questions.s: Concerning the sciatic nerve in the buttock (Last's):
o: The artery to the sciatic nerve is the remnant of the axial artery
From the inferior gluteal. (Last's p. 163)
The sciatic nerve emerges medial to the pudendal nerve
It emerges more laterally than the inferior gluteal and pudendal. (Last's p. 164)
The sciatic nerve touches bone a third of the way up from ischial tuberosity to PSIS
Its surface marking of entry. (Last's p. 164)
In a high division the tibial nerve pierces piriformis
The common peroneal does. (Last's p. 164)
The nerve to quadratus femoris lies deep to obturator internus and the gemelli
Separating it from the sciatic nerve. (Last's p. 164)
The inferior gemellus is supplied by the nerve to obturator internus
By the nerve to quadratus femoris; the superior by the nerve to obturator internus. (Last's p. 164)
The quadrate tubercle is not produced by the pull of quadratus femoris
It marks the greater trochanter epiphyseal fusion. (Last's p. 165)
The internal pudendal artery lies medial to the pudendal nerve
It lies lateral to the nerve. (Last's p. 164)
Last's says the iliofemoral ligament is an inverted V, not a Y
Bigelow never described a Y. (Last's p. 166)
The transverse acetabular ligament contains cartilage cells like the labrum
Unlike the labrum it has none. (Last's p. 165-6)
Posteriorly the hip capsule attaches halfway along the femoral neck
Anteriorly to the intertrochanteric line. (Last's p. 166)
The ischiofemoral ligament is the strongest hip ligament
It is the weakest; the iliofemoral is strongest. (Last's p. 166)
The popliteal vein lies between artery and nerve at all levels
(Last's p. 172-4)
The sural nerve is usually medial to the small saphenous vein
It is usually lateral. (Last's p. 173)
The recurrent genicular nerve supplies upper lateral fibres of tibialis anterior
(Last's p. 173)
The popliteal artery is about 10 cm long
About 20 cm, hiatus to soleal arch. (Last's p. 174)
The sural arteries are end-arteries
Severing them causes necrosis of gastrocnemius heads. (Last's p. 174)
The popliteal artery enters the fossa lateral to the sciatic nerve
It enters medial and deep, then becomes lateral to the tibial nerve. (Last's p. 174)
The middle genicular nerve pierces the oblique popliteal ligament to the cruciates
(Last's p. 173)
The genicular branches of the tibial nerve supply the lateral capsule
They supply the medial capsule; the common peroneal supplies the lateral. (Last's p. 173)

questions.s: Concerning lower limb nerve supply and injury (Last's):
o: The medial plantar nerve usually supplies three and a half digits
Like the median in the hand. (Last's p. 212)
Lower limb sympathetic preganglionics arise from T1–T6
From T11–L2. (Last's p. 213)
Femoral nerve injury is more likely from lower abdominal than limb wounds
It breaks into branches as soon as it enters the thigh. (Last's p. 213)
In obturator palsy loss of adduction is obvious during walking
It is unnoticed in walking; the leg cannot be crossed when sitting. (Last's p. 213)
Sciatic injury occurs in about 7% of hip dislocations
And 16% of fracture-dislocations. (Last's p. 213)
Sciatic nerve injury alone causes anaesthesia on the back of the thigh
Only if the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve is also damaged. (Last's p. 213)
The saphenous nerve may be ligated in varicose vein surgery in front of the medial malleolus
(Last's p. 214)
Common peroneal lesions always cause marked sensory loss
Like radial lesions, there may be little or none. (Last's p. 214)
Last's calls the sacral plexus the true plexus of the lower limb
The lumbar plexus supplies parts "borrowed from the trunk". (Last's p. 414)
The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve supplies the testis
It does not, and is unlikely to supply scrotal skin. (Last's p. 415)
The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve supplies the peritoneum of the iliac fossa
It is mostly L2. (Last's p. 415)
The femoral part of the genitofemoral is L2
The femoral part is L1, genital L2. (Last's p. 415)
The lateral femoral circumflex artery divides femoral branches into superficial and deep
(Last's p. 415)
The nerve to pectineus passes in front of the femoral sheath
It runs behind the sheath. (Last's p. 415)
The nerve to vastus medialis carries most femoral fibres to the knee
(Last's p. 415)
The nerve to rectus femoris is usually single
It is usually double; the upper branch supplies the hip. (Last's p. 415)
The obturator nerve lies on the sacral ala lateral to the lumbosacral trunk
(Last's p. 416)
The anterior division of the obturator pierces obturator externus
The posterior division does. (Last's p. 416)
A branch of the posterior division accompanies the femoral artery to the knee
(Last's p. 416)
The posterior division supplies gracilis
The anterior division supplies gracilis. (Last's p. 416)

questions.s: Concerning branches of the sacral plexus (Last's):
o: The posterior femoral cutaneous nerve stays beneath the deep fascia
Unique; it reaches mid-calf. (Last's p. 416)
The perforating cutaneous nerve passes through the greater sciatic foramen with the sciatic
It pierces the sacrotuberous ligament. (Last's p. 416)
The inferior rectal nerve does not supply levator ani
It supplies the external anal sphincter. (Last's p. 417)
Levator ani is supplied mainly by the pudendal nerve
By the perineal branch of S4 on its upper surface. (Last's p. 417)
The nerve to quadratus femoris has the same roots as the superior gluteal
The common peroneal part of the sciatic is formed from all five posterior divisions
From four (L4–S2); the tibial from all five (L4–S3). (Last's p. 417)
If fusion fails the common peroneal pierces piriformis
(Last's p. 417)
The nerve to obturator internus supplies the inferior gemellus
It supplies the superior; quadratus femoris nerve supplies the inferior. (Last's p. 417)
The common peroneal nerve itself supplies no muscles
(Last's p. 418)
The superficial peroneal pierces the deep fascia about a third of the way down the leg
It emerges from peroneus longus a third down but pierces the fascia about halfway. (Last's p. 418)
The deep peroneal nerve runs lateral to the anterior tibial vessels
(Last's p. 418)
The sural nerve pierces the deep fascia in the popliteal fossa
It pierces it halfway down the leg. (Last's p. 418)
